title: 3. Assignment: Write a Popular Scientific Summary About a Citizen Science Project
text:
Assignment time: 1h 15 min 

Objective
In this assignment, you will explore a Swedish citizen science project and practice translating complex research into an engaging and accessible format. This will help you develop essential science communication skills while deepening your understanding of citizen science in Sweden.


Step 1: Choose a Citizen Science Project
Find a Swedish citizen science project that interests you and that you would like to learn more about. The project can be either ongoing or already completed.
Examples of projects can be found on medborgarforskning.se under the heading ‘Medborgarforskningsprojekt’. You’re also welcome to choose a project that’s not on this list!


Step 2: Analyze the Project
Once you have chosen a project, analyze it using the following guiding questions:

What is the project’s goal? – What scientific question or problem does it aim to address?
Who are the participants, and how do they contribute? – What role does the public play in the research?

How are the results communicated to the public? – Does the project engage participants beyond data collection?

Is this an example of good science communication? Why or why not? – Consider clarity, accessibility, and engagement strategies.

Please submit your analysis in this Google form.


Step 3: Write a Popular Science Article
Using your analysis, write a ~500-word popular science article about the project. Your article should:

Be engaging and accessible to a non-expert audience
Clearly explain the project’s purpose and impact
Use storytelling techniques or real-world examples to make the science relatable

Please submit your article in this Google form.

title: 1. Introduction to Science Communication and Citizen Science
text:
Reading time: 15 min 

Science communication
Science isn’t just for scientists—it belongs to everyone! As a researcher, your work has the power to shape society, influence policy, and inspire future generations. But for that to happen, people need to understand and engage with your research. That’s where science communication comes in.
Science communication is the practice of sharing scientific knowledge, methods, and discoveries with audiences beyond the academic community. This includes engaging with:

the public
policymakers

journalists

industry stakeholders

through various channels, such as:

media articles

social media

public lectures

exhibitions
citizen science initiatives

Here’s why it matters:
🌍 Impact & Influence – Your research can inform policies, healthcare, and innovation—but only if the right people understand it.
🧭 Public Trust in Science – Misinformation spreads fast. Clear, transparent communication helps build trust in scientific research.
🤝 Collaboration & New Perspectives – Engaging with the public and industry can bring fresh insights, making your research more inclusive and applicable.
Unlike in many other countries, science communication isn’t just encouraged in Sweden—it’s legally required. The Higher Education Act (1992:1434), established science communication as the tredje uppgift (third mission), which means universities must share their knowledge with society. In short, if you’re a researcher in Sweden, you have a responsibility to communicate your work beyond academia.
Luckily, you’re not alone in communicating your science! Sweden has a strong network of organizations that promote and support science communication, for example:

Vetenskap & Allmänhet (Public & Science Sweden) – a national non-profit organization with around 100 member institutions. Helps researchers engage with the public and policymakers through events, training, and outreach projects.

Forskom (Sweden’s Network for Research Communication) – A community for science communicators to exchange ideas and strategies.

Falling Walls Engage Hub Sweden – Connects science communicators across the Nordic region to share best practices and create innovative engagement projects.

In addition, most universities in Sweden have dedicated communication teams that can help you share your work through media, social platforms, and public engagement events. Here are a few examples:

SciLifeLab. The SciLifeLab operations office has communication officers who can support you with public outreach.

Karolinska Institutet. Provides tools and guidance to support you with communication work.

University of Gothenburg. Has a press office and press contacts per faculty.

Stockholm University. Offers structured communication support for researchers.

Science communication is also recognized by funders as an essential part of research. Major funding includes:

Vetenskapsrådet – Offers grants for research communication and runs forskning.se, a public science platform.

Vinnova – Funds innovation-focused research and emphasizes societal impact.

Wallenberg Foundations – Sweden’s largest private research funders, which prioritize research dissemination.



Citizen science
Citizen science can be considered to be the ultimate form of science communication — it doesn’t just share research with the public, it invites people to actively participate in research. For you as a researcher, this means a direct connection with society, making your work more open, transparent, and impactful.
Citizen science is a research approach that actively involves non-scientists in scientific investigations. Participants can contribute by collecting data, analyzing results, or even co-designing studies. It can take many forms—volunteers monitoring biodiversity, communities tracking air quality, or gamers helping to fold proteins in an online puzzle. These projects don’t just advance research; they make science accessible and engaging, allowing you to build trust with the public and expand the reach of your work.
Sweden has a strong and growing citizen science community, with projects spanning biodiversity monitoring, environmental research, health sciences, and digital humanities. Vetenskap & Allmänhet plays a key role in promoting citizen science in Sweden by coordinating various projects that engage the public in hands-on research. Examples include The Plastic Experiment, The Star-Spotting Experiment, and The Food Waste Experiment (Svinnkollen).
Other examples of citizen science in Sweden include:

Artportalen: A biodiversity citizen science platform where the public reports observations of species, helping scientists track environmental changes. Researchers communicate findings back to contributors, creating a feedback loop.

​​BatMapper: This project enlists volunteers to gather data on bat activity and roosting sites across Sweden. Participants assist in collecting essential information that aids researchers in understanding bat populations and their responses to environmental changes.

Naturens kalender: This project collects phenological observations of plants and birds throughout Sweden. Participants monitor events like flowering, fruit ripening, and bird appearances, contributing to studies on climate change impacts.

Luftdata: A citizen science project that enables individuals across Sweden to contribute to air quality monitoring by building and installing their own low-cost air pollution sensors. The collected data is openly shared, providing real-time insights into particulate matter (PM) levels and helping scientists, policymakers, and the public understand local air pollution trends.

 In this module, you’ll dive into the essentials of science communication — why it matters, how it’s practiced, and its crucial role in open science and citizen engagement. You’ll discover how to effectively communicate your research to different audiences, and explore how citizen science takes science communication to the next level by actively involving the public in research.
To get hands-on experience with science communication and citizen science, you’ll choose a Swedish citizen science project and create a popular scientific summary that translates complex research into an engaging, accessible format. This hands-on exercise will help you develop a key skill for making your science more open, transparent, and impactful.

title: 4. GRP in (inter)national collaboration
text:
Reading time: 7 min                                    Reflection question #: 6, 7 
As a researcher, collaboration is key to innovation—whether you’re working with fellow academics, industry partners, or international teams. Engaging in responsible collaboration ensures that research remains transparent, ethical, and legally compliant, while fostering creativity and meaningful impact.
The following sections provide practical guidance on how to uphold GRP in collaborative research settings.

Collaboration with non-academic actors in society
Research often extends beyond academia, involving partnerships with government agencies, businesses, NGOs, and other societal actors. These collaborations allow you to:

address complex societal challenges

co-create knowledge

develop innovative solutions

ensure research has real-world applications and benefits

However, working with external actors requires careful attention to:

Clearly defining responsibilities to maintain transparency and accountability

Monitoring research impact beyond the primary study focus, especially regarding the operations of partner organizations

Recognizing and mitigating power imbalances that could influence the research process or affect stakeholders

By proactively addressing these aspects, you can ensure ethical and impactful collaboration that benefits both research and society.



International collaboration
Exchanging knowledge and/or material across borders enriches research but also introduces ethical, legal, and cultural complexities. To engage in “responsible internationalization” (see STINT for more information), you and your institution should:

Identify and adhere to relevant ethical regulations in all involved countries, ensuring research planning aligns with these standards.
Avoid so called “ethical dumping”, upholding Swedish ethical standards even when local regulations are more permissive, to protect people, animals, and the environment.
Clearly define ownership and intellectual property rights, ensuring fair handling of data, materials, and research findings.
Establish conflict-resolution mechanisms to address ethical breaches or deviations from GRP.

For structured guidance, the Association of Swedish Higher Education Institutions (SUHF) provides a checklist to help navigate ethical concerns, while the TRUST code promotes equitable global research partnerships.

If your research involves genetic resources or traditional knowledge from another country, compliance with:

the Nagoya Protocol

EU Access and Benefit Sharing Regulation

National laws of the supplier country
is mandatory.

When dealing with indigenous data, applying the CARE principles ensures ethical and respectful governance. You must document compliance with relevant regulations in the supplier’s country, using tools like EU DECLARE. For further support, visit Naturvårdsverket.
By integrating these practices into your collaborative efforts, you contribute to ethical, globally responsible research that fosters trust, innovation, and positive impact.

title: Course syllabus
text:
Course content
The 1hp course ‘Open Science in the Swedish Context’ is designed to teach DDLS research school scientists how to apply Swedish Open Science standards in their daily research. The course covers key stages of the research lifecycle, from planning a research project, to sharing results, to science communication and researcher evaluation. Through interactive lectures, guest speakers, and practical assignments, participants will explore pre-registration, Open Access publishing, up-and-coming researcher evaluation criteria, and citizen science. Completing this training will prepare DDLS students to lead the global shift toward open and collaborative research.

Demonstrate an understanding of ethical principles and legal frameworks governing research in Sweden

title: 1. Introduction to Good Research Practice
text:
Reading time: 7 min                                    Reflection question #: 1, 2 
As a researcher, you are responsible for conducting your work with integrity, ensuring that your methods and findings are ethical, reliable, and credible. Good Research Practice (GRP) is defined as “the collective ethical criteria on how good research should be conducted” (VR, 2024), and includes a set of ethical standards and guidelines that shape research practices across various disciplines. It provides the ethical and professional foundation for research across all disciplines, thereby ensuring the credibility and reliability of your research findings, safeguarding public trust in science, upholding the well-being of research subjects, and respecting the broader societal impact of discoveries you make. Simply put, producing high-quality research is impossible without a strong commitment to GRP (VR, 2024).

Your legal and ethical responsibilities
In Sweden, following GRP is not just an ethical obligation—it is a legal requirement. As a researcher, you must comply with national legislation, including:

Law 2019:504. the Act on Responsibility for Good Research Practice and the Examination of Research Misconduct (‘lagen om ansvar för god forskningssed och prövning av oredlighet i forskning’)

In addition to legal frameworks, you must adhere to well-established integrity and ethics guidelines, such as:

Good Research Practice (‘God Forskningssed’)

The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity

and you also must follow broader ethical agreements that shape research integrity, including:

the Declaration of Helsinki

the Nagoya Protocol

Beyond these formal guidelines, your institution may have its own code of conduct, such as the SciLifeLab code of conduct.



What GRP Means for You in Practice
Upholding GRP is not just about avoiding misconduct—it is about actively engaging with ethical principles in every aspect of your research. This means:

Being aware of and following all relevant regulations that apply to your field.
Maintaining good research habits and making ethical decisions at every stage of your work.
Exercising sound professional judgment and resisting undue influence.
Continuously updating your knowledge to keep pace with evolving ethical and legal standards.



The Role of Your Institution
You are not solely responsible for maintaining GRP standards in your research project. Research-performing organizations play a crucial role in fostering an ethical research environment by (SUHF, 2023):

Providing training and mentorship to help you navigate GRP principles.
Offering support structures, such as clear ethical guidelines.
Ensuring infrastructure and technical support is in place, including well-defined procedures.
Creating incentives that reward adherence to GRP.

At the same time, Swedish law (Law 1992:1434. The higher education act (‘Högskolelag’)) dictates that your research performing organization has to guarantee you academic freedom. This freedom also means that part of the responsibility to uphold research integrity lies on you (Section 4 of Law 2019:504). Ethical considerations and legal requirements may vary across disciplines, so it is your duty to stay informed and apply GRP principles appropriately within your field.



What you need to succeed
To be a responsible researcher, you must develop key competencies, including:

A strong understanding of GRP principles and frameworks.
The ability to apply ethical guidelines in real-world research scenarios.
Good professional judgment and research habits.
The ability to resist pressures that could compromise integrity.
The skills to navigate ethical dilemmas with confidence.



What’s next?
The following chapters will guide you through how to apply GRP throughout an academic project—from securing funding to conducting experiments, collaborating nationally and internationally, publishing, and reviewing. Chapter 6 will cover research misconduct, including what happens if an accusation is made, and final Chapter 7 delves in to how GRP relates to Open Science principles.

title: Self-study: Pre-course assignments
text:
Introduction
Open Science is all about making scientific research, data, and knowledge available to everyone. It’s a global movement that encourages transparency, collaboration, and sharing ideas freely. This makes it easier for researchers to build on each other’s work, speed up innovation, and improve the trustworthiness and accuracy of research results.


The 4 key pillars Open Science is built on, and the areas within Open Science they refer to. Unesco (2022) Understanding Open Science, https://doi.org/10.54677/UTCD9302, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO



In Sweden, Open Science has become a big priority for the government, universities, and funding bodies in recent years. In 2017, the Swedish government tasked The Royal Library (Kungliga Biblioteket, KB) with leading the charge to make research publications freely accessible. The Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet, VR) has been tasked with making research data publicly available. These efforts have laid the groundwork for bringing Open Science practices into Swedish higher education.
Right now, Sweden is still in the process of fully transitioning to Open Science. To help guide this change, KB created the National Guidelines for Open Science, in which areas within Open Science that are prioritised and crucial to develop fully in Sweden are highlighted. These areas are:

Open access to scholarly publications

Open access to research data

Open research methods

Open educational resources

Public engagement in science

Infrastructures supporting open science

During the in-person workshop on March 20th, Module 1 will explore the state of Open Science in Sweden, especially focusing on the National Guidelines. This pre-course assignment is designed to help you get familiar with the guidelines before the workshop kicks off.

title: 2. GRP in acquiring funding
text:
Reading time: 3 min                                    Reflection question #: 3 
As a researcher, you have a responsibility to use research funding and resources both ethically and efficiently. This means striving to:

Maximize the value of your research while minimizing wasted time and resources.
Avoid unnecessary harm, risk, or suffering to people, animals, or the environment.

When applying for funding, your proposal should clearly demonstrate how your research has the potential to generate valuable knowledge and/or societal benefits. Conducting research without such potential goes against the principles of GRP.


Ethical Considerations in Grant Applications
When applying for grants—such as those from the the Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet), Horizon Europe, and the ERC, you must reflect on ethical aspects from the very beginning of your project. Grant applications require you to address both legal requirements and broader ethical concerns, including:

Identifying potential ethical challenges in your research.

Describing how these ethical issues will be managed throughout the project.

Ensuring compliance with relevant laws and regulations.

Justifying why your research should be conducted and its expected impact.

For guidance on integrating ethical considerations into your grant proposals, refer to resources such as: VR ‘Conducting ethical research’, Horizon Europe ‘Ethics self-assessment guide’, and ERC ‘Ethics guidance’.


Why This Matters
By addressing ethical issues transparently and comprehensively in your funding applications, you help foster trust, accountability, and responsible resource use in research. Ethical integrity in grant proposals not only strengthens your application but also reinforces the credibility of scientific work as a whole.

title: 5. GRP in publishing and reviewing
text:
Reading time: 7 min                                    Reflection question #: 8, 9 

Writing
As a researcher, your scientific publications are a primary way to share your findings with the world. Upholding GRP in publishing ensures that your work is transparent, honest, and responsible—building trust within the research community and beyond.
According to VR (2024), responsible scientific publishing means:

Presenting data, methods, results and interpretations in an open, honest, transparent and correct manner, while meeting the interest in protection and legitimate demands for confidentiality

clearly reporting study robustness, assumptions and values, sources of error and remaining uncertainties and knowledge gaps

referring and citing clearly and correctly, in accordance with the standard that applies to the research area

openly reporting any conflicts of interest, financial support and dependencies

preventing the dissemination and use of incorrect results or misleading information

By following these principles, you ensure that your research is credible, reproducible, and impactful.


Authorship
Determining authorship can be one of the most sensitive aspects of publishing. The Vancouver recommendations provide a clear four-step framework to define who qualifies as a co-author. To be listed, a researcher must:

Make a substantial contribution to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data for the work; AND

Write or critically revise the manuscript for intellectual content; AND

Approve the final version before submission; AND

Take responsibility for the integrity of all aspects of the work and be accountable for any concerns about accuracy


If you use AI tools to generate text or content, you must disclose this and ensure that AI-generated contributions are reliable and ethically integrated into your work.


Journal selection
When selecting a journal, prioritize those that uphold rigorous peer-review standards. Avoid journals that lack transparency in their review process, charge hidden fees, or compromise on quality.
Ensure your research is accessible to both peers and the public as soon as possible, while respecting legitimate delays—such as those related to patent applications.


Peer review
If you are reviewing manuscripts from peers, you play a critical role in maintaining research quality. Ethical peer review, as outlined by the Committee on Publication Ethics’ (COPE) ethical guidelines, requires that you:

Provide an honest assessment

Provide a well-founded assessment

Disclose any conflicts of interest that could bias your review

Refrain from participating if there is a risk of undue influence


Researchers must also help counteract publication bias by supporting the publication of valid studies, regardless of whether the results confirm or reject a hypothesis

title: 3. GRP in experimental research
text:
Reading time: 15 min                                    Reflection question #: 4, 5 
As a researcher, you play a key role in upholding ethical standards when conducting experiments. Ethical research isn’t just a requirement—it’s the foundation of trust, integrity, and scientific progress. The ALLEA Code outlines four fundamental principles that apply to all research, regardless of discipline:

Reliability in ensuring the quality of research, reflected in the design, methodology, analysis, and use of resources

Honesty in developing, undertaking, reviewing, reporting, and communicating research in a transparent, fair, full, and unbiased way

Respect for colleagues, research participants, research subjects, society, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and the environment

Accountability for the research from idea to publication, for its management and organisation, for training, supervision, and mentoring, and for its wider societal impacts


When you conduct research, it’s essential to carefully balance several legitimate interests (VR, 2024):

the pursuit of valuable knowledge

the protection of those affected by research

the promotion of openness and transparency

the maintenance of trust in the research process

Among these, the protection interest always comes first. This means prioritizing the health, safety, and well-being of everyone involved, whether they are research participants or others impacted by your work. Their protection is paramount and must take precedence over all other considerations.
Research often carries direct risks. These might include physical interventions, such as surgeries or administering drugs; psychological distress caused by the research process; or the mishandling of sensitive materials or data. As a researcher, it’s your responsibility to be fully aware of these risks and to take every possible step to mitigate them.

In addition to these general foundations of GPR in conducting research, there are various specific areas of research ethics that we’ll explore further in the following sections:


Research involving humans

When your research involves humans—whether through interviews, observations, interventions, experiments, or data collection (such as personal data)—you must follow strict ethical guidelines and ensure your study undergoes an ethical review. Ethical oversight is not optional; it is a fundamental requirement for responsible research.
A strong ethical foundation for human research is built on the four principles of medical ethics:

To do good – Your research should aim to benefit individuals or society

To do no harm – You must minimize risks and avoid unnecessary harm

To respect self-determination - Participants must provide informed consent and have autonomy over their involvement

To uphold justice - The benefits and burdens of research should be distributed fairly

Further essential guidelines for conducting ethical human research are provided in the Declaration of Helsinki and the Swedish Ethical Review Act (2003:460 ‘Om etikprövning av forskning som avser människor’).

Conducting Clinical Studies in Sweden
If your research involves clinical studies, you must comply with EU Regulation 536/2014. Additionally, if your study is funded by certain agencies (such as the Swedish Research Council, VR), it must be registered in public databases like ClinicalTrials.gov or Researchweb.
For clinical research involving ionizing radiation, you must also seek approval from a local radiation protection committee in accordance with the Swedish Radiation Safety Authority’s regulations(‘Strålsäkerhetsmyndigheten’, SSMFS 2018:1).


Ethical Approval for Other Human Studies
If your research involves humans but is not classified as a clinical study, you must apply for ethical approval through the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (‘Etikprövningsmyndigheten’). They provide a detailed guideline outlining:
- The relevant laws governing research ethics
- How to determine whether your study requires ethical review
- The process for applying for approval
If your application is denied, you have the right to appeal to the Ethics Review Appeals Board (‘Överklagandenämnden för etikprövning’).


Accessing Human Samples for Research
If your study requires human biological samples, you need both ethical approval and a biobank application. The Biobank Act (2023:38, ‘Biobankslag’) outlines the legal framework for accessing and storing human biological material. You can apply for biobank access through Biobank Sweden.
By following these ethical requirements, you ensure that your research is conducted responsibly, transparently, and with respect for the individuals involved.



Research involving animals

If your research involves laboratory animals, you must follow strict ethical and legal guidelines to ensure responsible and humane treatment. In Sweden, animal research is governed by:
- the Animal Welfare Act (2018:1192 ‘Djurskyddslag’)
- the Animal Welfare Ordinance (2019:66, ‘Djurskyddsförordning’)
- regulations from the Swedish Board of Agriculture (SJVFS 2019:9)
Only animals specifically bred for research purposes (destination breeding) are permitted for use in experiments.


Obtaining Ethical Approval
Before you begin any animal experiments, you must secure ethical approval from a regional animal experimentation ethics committee. This requires submitting an application through an e-service provided by the Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket). Once approved, experiments can only be conducted by researchers or staff with formal training in Laboratory Animal Science (LAS).


Following the 3R Principles
As outlined by the Swedish 3R center, all animal research must follow the 3Rs principle to promote ethical practices::

Replace animal use where possible

Reduce the number of animals used

Refine methods to minimize suffering

You are responsible for designing your experiments in a way that prioritizes animal welfare while maintaining scientific integrity. To ensure best practices, refer to internationally recognized guidelines such as PREPARE and ARRIVE.



Genetic engineering

If your research involves genetic engineering, you must adhere to strict safety, ethical, and environmental regulations. In Sweden, genetic research is governed by several key laws, ensuring responsible scientific practice

2006:351 on Genetic Integrity etc. ‘Om genetisk integritet m.m.’

2002:1086 on the Release of Genetically Modified Organisms into the Environment ‘Om utsättning av genetiskt modifierade organismer i miljön’

2000:271 on the Contained Use of Genetically Modified Organisms ‘Om innesluten användning av genetiskt modifierade organismer’
DS2000:61 the Swedish Environmental Code



Navigating Regulations and Ethical Considerations
As a researcher, you are responsible for ensuring compliance with these legal frameworks and ethical standards. Different authorities provide guidance and oversight, depending on your area of study:

Swedish Board of Agriculture (‘Jordbruksverket’) - Regulations on genetic modification (GMOs) in agriculture

Medical Products Agency (‘Läkemedelsverket’) – Oversight of gene therapies and medical applications

the Swedish Work Environment Authority (‘Arbetsmiljöverket’) - Responsible for the Environmental Code when it comes to issues of genetic engineering

the Gene Technology Advisory Board (‘Gentekniknämnden’) - Provides expert guidance on ethically justifiable and safe use of gene technology

the National Council on Medical Ethics (‘Statens medicinsk-etiska råd’) – Addresses ethical dilemmas in genetic research




Development/use of certain types of technology

If your research involves working with emerging, cutting-edge technologies, you play a crucial role in navigating the ethical challenges that come with innovation. The rapid advancement and widespread adoption of new technologies can sometimes outpace critical ethical discussions, raising important questions about their responsible use.
To ensure that your research aligns with ethical best practices, you should proactively reflect on the broader implications of your work. Consider the potential risks, unintended consequences, and societal impact of the technologies you develop. What safeguards should be in place? Who might be affected by your research, and how?
For further guidance, explore the ethical considerations outlined in VR, 2024. By addressing these challenges early, you contribute to the responsible and sustainable development of technology.



Dual-use items

As a researcher, you may work with products, technologies, or information that have both civilian and military applications—these are known as dual-use items (produkter med dubbla användningsområden, PDA). Because of their potential for misuse, strict regulations govern their development, handling, and export.
To ensure compliance and prevent unintended consequences, you must follow both European (EU 2021/821, EU 2021/1700) and Swedish (Act 2000:1064) regulations.
To navigate these rules effectively, refer to the Inspectorate for Strategic Products (Inspektionen för strategiska produkter) which provides further guidance on research and export controls. By staying informed and compliant, you help ensure that your research is used responsibly and ethically.



Artificial intelligence

When incorporating AI tools into your research, you must carefully navigate issues of privacy, confidentiality, and intellectual property rights—especially when working with sensitive or personal data. Within the EU, AI usage is governed by specific legislation, nd the European Commission has provided guidelines on AI ethics and responsible use in research.
To ensure that your research remains ethical and compliant, it is essential to follow data protection laws and adhere to established guidelines when integrating AI into your work. By doing so, you help safeguard trust, integrity, and accountability in research involving AI.



Processing of personal data (GDPR)

When working with personal data in research, you must navigate strict legal and ethical requirements to protect individuals’ rights and privacy. The EU General Data Protection Regulation GDPR (2016/679 EU Data Protection Regulation) along with Sweden’s national regulations (2018:218 Supplementary provisions to the EU General Data Protection Regulation, ‘Kompletterande bestämmelser till EU:s dataskyddsförordning’) set the framework for handling personal data in research.
If your research involves processing personal data, you are required to register your project with your university’s data protection officer (‘dataskyddsombud’). Personal data includes any information that can be traced back to a living individual—even if additional data (such as a code key, text material, or an audio recording) is needed for identification.
Beyond the core GDPR principles outlined in Article 5 of the GDPR, Article 89.1 establishes specific rules for processing personal data in research to safeguard individuals’ rights and freedoms. If your study involves sensitive personal data or data related to legal violations, additional legal safeguards apply. In these cases, you must obtain ethical approval under the Swedish Ethical Review Act before beginning your research.
By staying informed and compliant, you help ensure that your research respects privacy, maintains trust, and upholds the highest ethical standards.

title: 6. Scientific misconduct
text:
Reading time: 10 min                                    Reflection question #: 10, 11 
As a researcher, upholding GRP is essential—not just for producing credible results, but also for maintaining public trust, ensuring ethical integrity, and fulfilling your societal responsibility. Yet, various pressures can lead to deviations from the laws, guidelines, and principles outlined in chapters 1-5.
Within the scientific community, several elements increase the likelihood that researchers might deviate from GRP. One major challenge is the competitive nature of research, which can create pressure to cut corners. Additionally, evaluation systems that focus on quantitative indicators —such as publication counts and citation metrics— may incentivize questionable shortcuts. Recognizing these risks and understanding how to mitigate them is crucial to maintaining research integrity.

In some cases, deviations from GRP may be unintentional, resulting from:

Ignorance: Lack of awareness of ethical research practices

Negligence: Carelessness in methodology or reporting

Stress and Pressure: High expectations, deadlines, or resource limitations

Poor Research Habits: Developing methods or attitudes inconsistent with ethical guidelines

However, in more serious instances, some researchers may intentionally bypass ethical practices to manipulate outcomes.

Understanding Research Misconduct
Under Act 2019:504, research misconduct is defined as:
“a serious deviation from good research practice in the form of fabrication, falsification or plagiarism committed intentionally or through gross negligence in the planning, implementation or reporting of research”
These core types of misconduct—often referred to as FFP (Fabrication, Falsification, and Plagiarism)—include:

Fabrication: Creating false data or results and presenting them as real.
Falsification: Manipulating materials, equipment, processes, or data to misrepresent the research. Includes changing, omitting or suppressing data without justification.
Plagiarism: Using another person’s ideas, processes, results, or words without proper attribution, thus violating intellectual property rights.

While fabrication and falsification almost always constitute research misconduct, plagiarism may not be considered a serious breach if it occurs unintentionally or without gross negligence.
Beyond FFP, there are other questionable research practices that violate GRP, such as:

Failing to verify sources or data adequately

Conducting insufficient experiments to ensure reliability

Misattributing authorship in publications

Reusing one’s own prior work without proper acknowledgment

Presenting results inaccurately or incompletely

Concealing AI use in content creation

Refusing to share results without valid reasons

Misrepresenting statistical significance

Hindering the research efforts of peers




What Happens When Research Misconduct is Suspected?
If misconduct is suspected, the case is handled according to Act 2019:504. The process depends on the severity of the case:

For serious cases (FFP), the National Board for the Assessment of Research Misconduct (Npof) (Nämnden för prövning av oredlighet i forskning) investigates the case.

For other deviations from GRP, The case is handled by your research institution (such as a university) under the Higher Education Ordinance (1993:100) (Högskoleförordningen). Institutions are required to establish clear guidelines for such examinations according to recommendations from SUHF.

There are three ways in which a report of suspicion of misconduct can be initiated at Npof:

Through a submission from a research performing organization
Through a direct notification from an individual (i.e. a whistleblower)
On Npofs initiative based on its own observations

Act 2021:890 on whistleblower protection ensures safeguards for those reporting suspected misconduct. Further guidance is available in the Whistleblower Protection Handbook.


What Are the Consequences of Research Misconduct?
After a case has been investigated according to procedure at Npof or a higher education institution, a decision on a deviation from GRP can have various consequences, such as:

Employment sanctions:

warnings

salary deductions

dismissal from position


Academic sanctions:

correction or withdrawal of published articles

suspension or withdrawal of grant funding

limitation to the ability of researchers to apply for or receive new grants


Legal consequences:

reprimands, warnings, injunctions, prohibitions, fines, administrative sanctions
in severe cases: imprisonment (e.g., for conducting research without necessary permits)


But beyond individual consequences, research misconduct has wider implications:

Erosion of public trust in science

Wasted resources on unreliable studies

Potential harm to people, animals, or the environment



Your Role in Upholding Research Integrity
As a researcher, your responsibility goes beyond simply avoiding misconduct—you must actively promote transparency, accountability, and high ethical standards in your work. By staying informed and committed to Good Research Practice, you contribute to the integrity of science and the trust society places in it.

title: 7. GRP and Open Science
text:
Reading time: 7 min                                    Reflection question #: 12,13 

Why Open Science?
As a researcher, your work contributes to the vast, interconnected world of knowledge. But how valuable is that contribution if your methods, data, and findings remain behind closed doors? Open Science is about sharing—making your research accessible, transparent, and reusable.
By openly sharing methods, protocols, data, results, publications, and educational materials, you can:

Enhance research quality – Open scrutiny helps reduce errors and strengthens scientific rigor.

Build public trust – Transparency fosters accountability and confidence in scientific findings.

Minimize publication bias – Avoid selective reporting and unnecessary duplication of studies.

Enable better collaboration – Open access to resources leads to more efficient, impactful research.

For these reasons, GRP encourages you to share as much insight into your work as possible. However, openness must be balanced with responsibility. This principle is summed up as:
“As open as possible, as closed as necessary.”



Public Access to Research: “Allmän handling”
In Sweden, research transparency isn’t just an ethical choice — it’s a legal obligation. The Freedom of the Press Ordinance (1949:105) (‘Tryckfrihetsförordning’), guarantees the public’s (‘allmänhetens’) right to access government documents (‘allmänna handlingar’), including those held by universities and research institutions.
This means:
📂 Most research documents are public – Meeting minutes, databases, email correspondence, and research protocols can be requested by anyone.
🙋 Anyone can request access – A requester does not have to provide a reason and can remain anonymous.
⚖️ Authorities must justify restrictions – If access is denied, the decision can be challenged in the Court of Appeal (‘Hovrätt’).
📜 Under the Archives Act (1990:782 ‘Arkivlag’), public research documents must be preserved and maintained for future legal, scientific, and historical purposes.
The right to access public documents can only be limited by the Public Access and Secrecy Act (2009:400 ‘Offentlighets- och sekretesslag’), which outlines what information must be kept confidential and is not available to the public, even upon request.


Data Sharing: The Heart of Open Science
Data is the foundation of research, but without access, its potential remains untapped. That’s why data sharing is a core principle of Open Science. In Sweden, Act 2022:818 (On the public sector’s access to data (‘Om den offentliga sektorns tillgängliggörande av data’)) encourages the public sector —including universities— to make research data as openly available as possible. To maximize the impact of your data, you should follow the FAIR principles:

Findable – Clearly documented and easy to locate

Accessible – Available through standardized protocols

Interoperable – Compatible with other data formats and systems

Reusable – Well-described so others can validate and build upon it

To support you in this process, the Swedish Research Council provides guidelines for FAIR data management, as well as a template for the creation of data management plans.



Balancing Openness with Protection
While openness is crucial, you also have a duty to protect sensitive information. The Public Access and Secrecy Act (2009:400) limits how universities and researchers can share data to ensure:

Confidentiality – Protecting personal data and sensitive research topics

Legal compliance – Following ethical guidelines and applicable laws

Risk mitigation – Balancing transparency with security

When full data sharing isn’t possible, GRP recommends alternative approaches:

Sharing metadata only – Providing descriptions without releasing the data itself

Releasing partial datasets – Sharing non-sensitive sections of the data

Anonymizing sensitive data – Removing identifiable details while maintaining usability

If data must remain confidential, it should be securely stored and made available only upon request—after a confidentiality review if needed.
Additionally, some data is exempt from open access, including:

Data protected under intellectual property laws, such as Patent Law (1967:837)

Data owned by third parties and protected by Copyright Law (1960:729).

Open Science isn’t just a trend—it’s a movement shaping the future of research, deeply rooted in GRP. As a researcher, you play a key role in upholding GRP by fostering transparency, collaboration, and integrity in your work.
